title: Cross-module inlining, 40 NIR cap
evidence: The inlining oracle (D207): every short non-generic function of every module is lowered ahead of the program into a builder of its own, and a call to one that came out at forty NIR instructions or under, with at most one register result, is replaced by a copy of its body -- parameters become the arguments, returns become branches to the continuation, references are re-interned -- in module order on both link paths, so an executable linked from artifacts is still byte-identical. Only a release build inlines (D211): a debug build keeps every call a frame, as section 13's debug-info rule says, and `emit-em-all --release` is where the artifacts' body edges come from. The artifact records a body edge to every inlined callee of another module, and `--incremental` acts on it: link/incremental pins, in release, a body edit behind a signature edge keeping the dependent and one behind a body edge rebuilding it. The oracle is built twice, the second against the first, so a copy is two levels deep and carries the body edges of the body it copies (D212, link/inline_nested: a leaf's body edit rebuilds the module two copies up). `--inline-cap N` and `--explain` (D348): the cap re-evaluated at 0/20/40/80/160 on the compiler compiling 500k lines (forty retained: seven per cent faster than none, twenty as fast at five per cent less image, more buys nothing) and every oracle decision explained on request. The cap holds within a module as well and the oracle stays two levels deep, on D348's measurement (D788).

title: Incremental rebuild on the edge rule
evidence: `emit-em-all --incremental` (D205) lets section 12's edge rule decide per module: the artifact on disk stays when its source hash and build mode are unchanged (`--release` builds release artifacts, D211) and every recorded edge still matches the declaration it names in the target's fresh Interface, and is replaced otherwise; `kept`/`rebuilt` is printed per module. The decision is taken after checking and before lowering (D214): every hash an Interface carries comes from the checker -- a body hash is over the declaration's tokens -- so the fresh Interfaces are written from it alone, and a kept module is not lowered, selected or written at all. That is the saving: over the compiler's 31 modules a build with nothing changed takes 10 s against 34 s, and one with a body edit in `decimal` rebuilds `decimal` alone in 13 s, linking byte-equal to a clean build. An artifact holds the whole module now, not the functions this program reaches; the linker prunes. link/incremental pins unchanged sources kept, a body edit behind a signature edge rebuilding only its module with the linked result byte-equal to a clean build, and a signature edit rebuilding the dependent, on both platforms. The artifact path became usable at this size in D213: a CRC per read and a bit-loop `xor` under it had cost minutes. The checker settles the declarations first and the edge rule decides on them, so a kept module's bodies are not checked either, and the load-time checksum is table-driven (D224): a build with nothing changed is 4 s. What is left is the load itself -- every artifact read and widened to decide -- and the declarations of every module. `emit-executable --incremental` and `run --incremental` are the hot build (D319): the keep set settled after the declarations, the kept modules' bodies and code skipped, each fresh module's artifact written as it is selected, and the image linked from every module's artifact, byte for byte the cold build's; the compiler with nothing changed settles in 0.6 s and links in 1.0 s. At scale the artifact path walks a module's own rows and resolves through indexes, bytes are bytes and the NIR section is not written (D320): warm, nothing changed, the compiler builds in 1.1 s, a 500k-line program in 3.1 s and a 2M-line one in 12.6 s, each the cold build's image byte for byte. An unchanged module is not parsed unless something that changed imports it (D322, artifacts carry their imports, format 6): warm builds 0.86 s / 1.5 s / 6.1 s, and a leaf edit costs the warm build plus the module; with the manifest's digests carried on the artifact (D323, format 7) a release-built compiler builds itself warm in 0.24 s, 500k lines in 0.97 s, 2M in 4.0 s; with the artifacts read and validated on worker threads and the link reading through the bounds it holds (D324): 0.19 s / 0.36 s / 1.6 s A one-function edit rebuilds in 100–460 ms on both hosts with a release-built compiler, cold 650 ms, warm 100 ms (D789).

title: M3-02: SPIR-V emitter on the Vulkan 1.2 floor and the Vulkan compute runtime
evidence: The design and the split are D1610: NIR lowered without the CPU frame, private memory as word arrays, device addresses under PhysicalStorageBuffer64, one push constant holding the argument block's address. Row 1 (D1610): `emit-executable FILE ROOT spv none OUT` writes the program's kernels as one SPIR-V 1.5 module -- 32-bit scalars, device slices as two-word addresses (no Int64), the invocation ids, `if` and `ret`, NoContraction on every float result; saxpy's module ran bit-identically with the CPU on an NVIDIA RTX 3080 and an Intel Iris Xe and is pinned byte for byte in both suites (tests/conformance/spirv). Rows 2 and 3 (D1611): `e.gpu.vulkan` dynamically loads Vulkan, enumerates floor devices, owns mapped device-addressable buffers, pipelines and dispatch; `.Vulkan` is wired through `e.gpu`, and each kernel's dependency-linked `K$spirv` companion embeds its module for `gpu.launch`. `gpu_vulkan_raw` checks pinned saxpy bit for bit on every floor device or explicitly reports no device; `examples/saxpy.e` prints equal CPU and Vulkan checksums on an NVIDIA RTX 3080 and an Intel Iris Xe. Row 4 (D1612): the emitter writes structured nested `while` and `for` loops with `break` and one or several `continue` edges; NIR's private stack carries mutable values instead of SSA phis. `tests/conformance/spirv/loop.spv` passes Vulkan 1.2 validation and is pinned byte for byte; `gpu_vulkan_loop` matches every CPU/Vulkan result on an NVIDIA RTX 3080, an Intel Iris Xe and WSL's Vulkan device. Row 5 (D1613): f32 division and square root retain NoContraction FMA refinement and finish with exact u64 significand division or restoring square root, including normal/subnormal rounding, infinities and canonical NaNs; f32 kernels request DenormPreserve. `tests/conformance/spirv/float.spv` passes Vulkan 1.2 validation and is pinned byte for byte; `gpu_vulkan_float` matches 8,192 deterministic random and boundary vectors against the CPU on an NVIDIA RTX 3080 and Intel Iris Xe. Row 6 (D1614): 8-, 16- and 64-bit integer values, packed narrow private loads and stores, struct and array locals, by-value aggregate helper parameters, ordinary `OpFunctionCall` helpers and monomorphised generic instances. `tests/conformance/spirv/types.spv` passes Vulkan 1.2 validation and is pinned byte for byte; `gpu_vulkan_types` matches the CPU word for word on an NVIDIA RTX 3080, Intel Iris Xe and WSL's Vulkan device. Row 7 is partial (D1615): one module-wide Workgroup word block sized for its largest kernel, shared loads/stores and aggregate copies, `gpu.barrier`, both `gpu.memory_barrier` scopes, every scoped 32-bit atomic form and 64-bit device atomics. `tests/conformance/spirv/sync.spv` is pinned byte for byte; `gpu_vulkan_sync` matches CPU shared and atomic results on the RTX 3080, Iris Xe and WSL's Vulkan device. Row 7 subgroup coverage now includes identity and votes (D1720, D1721): `gpu.sid`, `gpu.subgroup_size()`, `gpu.subgroup_elect()`, `gpu.subgroup_all()`, `gpu.subgroup_any()` and `gpu.subgroup_ballot()` use the CPU's fixed 32-lane model and Vulkan's subgroup inputs plus Vote/Ballot operations. The CPU scheduler tags subgroup cuts separately from workgroup barriers, resumes independent subgroups, and snapshots predicates so every lane reads one completed vote. `tests/conformance/spirv/subgroup.spv` is pinned byte for byte; `gpu_subgroup_identity` validates full and partial subgroup votes and masks on the CPU, two Windows Vulkan devices and WSL's Vulkan device, and the complete Windows self-host suite passes. Capability discovery and launch refusal are now wired end to end (D1722): Vulkan queries integer, float, atomic, subgroup and f32 denormal support through `vkGetPhysicalDeviceProperties2` and feature records; `DeviceInfo.capabilities`, `gpu.has` and the generated launcher's inferred requirement mask use the same bits. `gpu_cpu` proves an unsupported `ftz` kernel is refused before execution; Windows runs each optional-capability fixture on its compatible adapter, WSL correctly leaves denormal-preserving float kernels on the CPU, and the complete Windows self-host suite passes. Broadcast and shuffle are now landed (D1723): typed 32/64-bit values cross the CPU's subgroup cut as snapshotted representation words, invalid or non-uniform sources trap, and SPIR-V emits the Ballot/Shuffle group operations. The pinned subgroup module is byte-identical across Windows and Linux; CPU, compatible Windows adapters and WSL pass full and partial subgroup checks. Row 7 is complete (D1725): integer add/min/max/and/or/xor and f32 add/min/max reuse the CPU snapshot and emit native SPIR-V arithmetic reductions; the pinned module is byte-identical across hosts, and the full/partial runtime fixture passes on the CPU, Windows Vulkan and WSL Vulkan, and the complete Windows self-host suite passes. Row 8 is partial (D1726-D1732): checked Vulkan launches carry a hidden fault-buffer address; bounds and slice guards use a device CAS so the first failure records its site and invocation, later failures count, and only the faulting invocation returns. Tag, enum, invalid and null trap blocks use the same writer and return. Pointer conditions collapse their two address words before the structured branch header, keeping `OpSelectionMerge` adjacent to `OpBranchConditional`. Debug integer add, subtract and multiply now guard their wrapped result for signed or unsigned overflow; divide and remainder always guard zero and signed `MIN / -1`, then record `Overflow` or `DivideByZero`. `gpu_fault_bounds` proves exact Bounds, Tag, Null, Alignment, Overflow and DivideByZero records, including null through a helper and every signed/unsigned arithmetic form, one-shot `sync`/`download`, `last_fault` and queue reuse on the CPU, two Windows Vulkan devices and WSL's Vulkan device. A module reserves the hidden slot only when reachable NIR can write a fault; its embedded companion marks that ABI, and `gpu_fault_nocheck` proves an all-`@nocheck` kernel starts ordinary parameters at byte zero on the CPU, two Windows Vulkan devices and WSL's Vulkan device. `gpu_fault_unchecked` builds a syntactically checked out-of-range access with `--unchecked`: CPU and Vulkan report no fault, exact Vulkan output proves the zero-prefix ABI, and both host manifests say `options.checks: off`. `spirv-val --target-env vulkan1.2` accepts both modules, their bytes are identical across Windows and Linux, and all six pinned SPIR-V modules remain unchanged. The full Windows suite remains blocked before compiler fixtures by the stale `docs/library-fixtures.json` produced by unrelated shared-tree library edits. Row 9 is partial (D1733): the Vulkan runtime persists one opaque driver blob per decoded SPIR-V xxHash64, entry point and device/driver/capability identity under the platform user cache or an isolated `NEPER_GPU_CACHE` root. Records carry magic, length and CRC-32C; a checksum-valid corrupt Vulkan header is rejected by the driver, rebuilt from an empty cache and durably atomically replaced only after pipeline success, while all cache I/O failures remain correctness-neutral misses. `gpu_vulkan_loop` restores the exact valid blob and CPU-identical output after that corruption on two Windows adapters and WSL's Vulkan device. The private `$spirv` companion now carries the writing compiler's executable/options identity (D1734), clean executable builds learn it, and `e.gpu` folds it into the cache key; changing only `--inline-cap` creates a distinct entry per device with the same CPU-identical result on Windows and WSL. Row 9 is complete (D1735): `gpu_cache_corrupt` injects a seeded rebuild failure after hashing the restored valid entry, requires a nonzero launch exit with that file byte-identical, then removes the injection and proves the cache remains usable on two Windows adapters and WSL's Vulkan device. Row 10 correctness is complete (D1736): GP-09's SIMD Base16 codec matches `e.bytes` for every tail length under the baseline and x64-v3 levels on Windows and Linux, while GP-10 maps the existing M3 corpus to its design obligations and keeps every exact compatible CPU/Vulkan result bit-identical on two Windows adapters and WSL. The comparison corpus and alternating standard-library runner are in place (D1737): C, C++, Rust, Go and Neper agree on both workload checksums, and Neper CPU/Vulkan agree on GP-10. The seven-run publication is complete (D1738): raw JSON and `docs/gp-performance.md` report every sample, compile/runtime p50 and p95, peak RSS and image size for all eleven C, C++, Rust, Go, Neper CPU and Neper Vulkan cells without hiding the measured optimisation gaps. The literal sweep now includes shared slices and pointers (D1739): NIR retains their address-space qualifier, `gpu_spaces` matches all eight CPU/Vulkan words on two Windows adapters and WSL's Vulkan device, and its raw module passes Vulkan 1.2 validation. The exact sweep also covers barriers and shared aggregates (D1740): `gpu_barrier` compares `relay`, looped `rounds`, and `plain`; `gpu_shared` compares integer `tally` everywhere and f32 `block_sum` where its denormal requirement is supported. It exposed and fixed contextual shared aggregate temporaries clobbering the workgroup block. All pass on two Windows adapters and WSL's Vulkan device. Packed private/shared bool spills are now emitted (D1741), making short-circuit kernels device-callable. `gpu_cpu` compares `ids` everywhere and `saxpy` on denormal-capable devices while checking `needs_ftz` capability/refusal; `gpu_present` compares every `fill` pixel. Both pass on two Windows adapters and WSL, and the raw module validates. The final exact-kernel audit is complete (D1742): `gpu_tensor` compares every reached u32 kernel, i64 where Int64 is present, and f32 where denormals are preserved on two Windows adapters and WSL. Undefined shared reads, deliberately divergent barriers, and compiler-statistics/incremental fixtures are explicitly outside the semantic comparison set. C090 is complete

title: Safety-signal detection in e.algo.stat

title: NeperOS 1a: an aarch64-none kernel image that boots on QEMU virt
evidence: Queued by D2125 when C099 closed; stage 1 of D2119; delivered in D2126. Acceptance: `--target aarch64-none` writes a raw image with the Linux arm64 Image header (magic `ARM\x64`, `text_offset`, `image_size` covering what the kernel zeroes) that `qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt -cpu cortex-a76 -kernel` loads and enters at EL1 with the device tree in `x0`, position-independent wherever the loader places it; no Linux runtime, only a boot stub that sets the stack, clears what the image does not carry and calls `main` with an arena carved from memory after the image; Neper reaches system registers (`mrs`/`msr`), barriers (`dsb`/`dmb`/`isb`), `wfi`/`wfe`, `hvc`/`smc` and volatile MMIO loads and stores through intrinsics that any other target refuses at check time; an exception vector table (sixteen entries, 2 KB aligned) saves the interrupted registers into a frame and calls a Neper handler; a kernel reads its memory and PL011 base from the device tree, turns on the MMU and caches with an identity map, writes to the PL011, and powers off through PSCI `SYSTEM_OFF` by the conduit the tree names. A fixture boots under QEMU on both hosts, checks the serial transcript, and takes a deliberate synchronous fault whose ESR and FAR the handler reports. A trap (bounds, overflow) reports its message and position on the console and powers off with a non-zero status. Delivered: `link_image_a64` writes the Image (header, code on a page, runtime 2 KB aligned, symbol table rebased to the image start, globals, and a bss for hook slots, a 256 KB stack and the arena -- 16 MB unless `--arena` says otherwise -- inside `image_size`); `runtime_none_a64.s` is the entry (FPEN on, vectors installed, the device tree as `args[0]`), the vectors and a 304-byte frame the handler may rewrite before `eret`, the console, exit and exception hooks (`os.set_console`, `os.set_exit`, `os.set_exception`), the trap printed through the console with its backtrace, and the machine as runtime calls seeded for aarch64-none alone: `load8`-`load64`, `store8`-`store64`, `barrier` (`dsb sy; isb`), `memory_barrier`, `tlb_flush`, `wait_for_interrupt`, `wait_for_event`, `send_event`, `hvc`, `smc`, and `mrs`/`msr` over a table of 45 system registers (anything else is reported and exits 136). Elsewhere `os.mrs` is refused where it is written (`E-NAME-9999`, fixture `kernel_refuse`). `em_link` resolves `aarch64-none` artifacts as aarch64 words, and `scripts/embed-elf-runtime.ps1 -Arch none` refuses a runtime with relocations. NeperOS is `neperos/src` (`fdt`, `pl011`, `psci`, `mmu`, `a64`, `main`): the 36 KB image finds the console through `/chosen`'s `stdout-path`, PSCI's conduit and RAM in the tree, maps the 39-bit space identity (Device gigabytes, 2 MB Normal write-back blocks over RAM), turns on the MMU and caches, reads past the 39-bit space and takes the translation fault (ESR 0x96000004), whose handler answers zero and steps over the load, then sends and waits for an event and powers off. Both suites boot it under qemu-system-aarch64 (QEMU 11.1 on Windows, 8.2 in WSL with `qemu-system-arm`, `-nic none`), check the transcript, and boot a copy loaded 2 MB higher (`text_offset` 4 MB) with `-append trap`, whose failed bounds check prints `trap[bounds]`, its position and `at main.main (src/main.e:...)`, and exits 134 through the kernel's PSCI hook. The first boot is the user's screenshot `welcome-neperos.png`. Both self-host suites pass.

title: NeperOS 1b: interrupts, the timer and preemptive threads at EL0
evidence: Queued by D2125 after C100; stage 1 of D2119; delivered in D2127. Acceptance: the GICv3 distributor and redistributors found in the device tree, the generic timer driving a preemptive round-robin scheduler, user threads at EL0 in their own translation tables (ASIDs, no shared kernel writable mappings, execute-never set), system calls by `svc`, and a QEMU fixture that runs EL0 threads interleaved by timer interrupts and kills one that touches kernel memory. Delivered: `gic` finds the controller at `/intc` (distributor and redistributor as its two `reg` regions, so `fdt.region_n`), turns on affinity routing and group 1, wakes the redistributor, and acknowledges/ends by `ICC_IAR1_EL1`/`ICC_EOIR1_EL1` through the registers already in the runtime table; `timer` arms the virtual timer (PPI 27) a hundredth of a second ahead. `thread` is a round-robin scheduler over a fixed table: a switch is a frame copy in place plus a `TTBR0_EL1` write, distinct ASIDs so no flush; the first tick captures the kernel's idle context and starts the first thread, the last to finish returns the kernel there and the boot loop powers off. `svc` gives console write (0, copied out of the caller's own bounds-checked region), exit (1) and yield (2). `vm` builds an address space as its own L1 over a copy of the kernel identity map plus one gigabyte at 0x80000000 mapped to the thread's pages EL0-RW and privileged-execute-never; the kernel's pages stay privileged-only, so an EL0 access into them faults -- the isolation. Page-table pages are over-allocated and aligned to 4 KB (an unaligned `TTBR0` broke the kernel's own fetch after the first switch). The user program is the new target `aarch64-neperos`: the same position-independent Image, `link_image_a64(program=true)` appending `runtime_neperos_a64.s` (entry from registers, console/exit/yield as `svc`s, `os.yield` the one extra intrinsic) and sizing `image_size` to the file; the header's first reserved word now carries the globals' offset. QEMU loads it with `-initrd`; the kernel reads `/chosen` `linux,initrd-start`/`-end`, copies it into three address spaces, and runs threads A, B and X. A and B interleave under the timer and finish; X, handed a second argument the kernel points at kernel RAM (0x40000000), faults on the read (EL0 permission abort) and is killed alone while A and B run on -- nothing forges a pointer, the kernel plants the one protected reference to prove the page tables stop it. Both suites build the program and kernel and boot them under `qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt,gic-version=3` on both hosts (QEMU 11.1 on Windows, 8.2 in WSL), check that all nine round tokens appear, that X is killed and never reads protected memory, and that the kernel powers off 0; the `trap` boot still ends 134 (handled before the controller and initrd). Both self-host suites pass.

title: NeperOS 1c: capabilities and synchronous IPC
evidence: Queued by D2125 after C101; stage 1 of D2119; delivered in D2128. Acceptance: every kernel object (untyped memory, thread, address space, endpoint, notification, IRQ handler, device frame) is reached only through a capability in the caller's capability space; untyped memory retypes into objects so the kernel allocates nothing after boot; endpoints carry synchronous IPC with capability transfer, notifications deliver interrupts to user drivers; capabilities derive with reduced rights and revoke recursively; the console moves to a user-mode server; a QEMU fixture checks that a thread without the console capability cannot print, that a derived read-only frame cannot be written, and that revocation reaches every derived capability. Delivered: each thread has a capability space (eight slots in its control block); endpoint, console, frame, notification, device and untyped objects are reached only through a capability with the right bits. Synchronous IPC over endpoint capabilities -- `send`/`recv` block and rendezvous (a new BLOCKED scheduler state the round-robin skips, the kernel idling when a block leaves nothing runnable), and carry one word plus an optional granted capability (transferred on the rendezvous when the endpoint capability has the grant right, a fresh root in the receiver's space). The console `write` is refused without a console capability; `cap_derive` copies with rights cleared and a parent link; `cap_revoke` nulls every capability derived from a slot through the chain; `frame_protect` walks the thread's own tables and flips a page's AP[1] by the frame capability's write right; a notification hands the timer interrupt to a user driver (the handler signals it before switching, the waiter wakes with the bits, the signaller never blocks); the console moves to a user-mode server K that alone holds the UART device capability and writes a client's line with `device_write` (one call, interrupts masked, so it is never split -- a raw EL0 store would be dropped as a dead store without a volatile the language lacks); and untyped memory retypes into objects (an untyped capability's budget bounds `retype`, which assigns an object slot reserved at boot, so the kernel allocates nothing afterward). Fourteen threads run together under the timer and prove it on both hosts under `-M virt,gic-version=3`: A/B/X interleave and X is killed reading kernel RAM (0x40000000); S/R rendezvous (R7 R8 R9); N without a console capability is refused and prints nothing; V derives a two-link chain, revokes the root and a receive on the revoked capability fails (V revoke ok); W derives a read-only frame capability, re-protects and faults on the next write (killed at 0x80040000); G grants its console capability to H, which held none and only then prints (H got console); D wakes three times on the timer notification (D0 D1 D2); K prints `console server up` for client P over its device capability; U retypes two endpoints from an untyped budget of two and the third is refused (U retype ok). Both suites check every expected line appears and none of the five boundary-crossing lines does; the `trap` boot still ends 134. New `aarch64-neperos` intrinsics `os.send`/`recv`/`cap_derive`/`cap_revoke`/`frame_protect`/`notify_wait`/`device_write`/`retype` (svc 3-10). Both self-host suites pass.

title: NeperOS 1d: virtio over PCI in user-mode drivers, closing stage 1
evidence: Queued by D2125 after C102; begun in D2129, transport and entropy driver in D2131, block driver in D2132, console transmit in D2133, EL0 memory-access surface in D2134, location-agnostic DMA pool in D2135, EL0 device-MMIO mapping in D2137, entropy driver as an EL0 user-mode server in D2138, all three drivers as EL0 servers in D2139, negative isolation prober in D2140, interrupt-driven drivers in D2141, console receive/echo and closure in D2142. Acceptance: the PCI ECAM window read from the device tree, the modern virtio-pci transport, and virtio console, block and entropy drivers running as EL0 servers that hold only their device's frames and interrupt; a QEMU fixture reads and writes a disk image and echoes the virtio console. Closing this item closes D2119 stage 1 and queues stage 2 (the AVF guest on a Pixel). Done (D2129): `pci` reads the generic ECAM host from `/pcie` (base 0x40_1000_0000 on virt, in gigabyte 256 the kernel's identity map covers as Device memory), addresses configuration space at `base + (bus<<20) + (slot<<15) + (function<<12) + offset`, reads vendor and device ids, and assigns BARs in the 32-bit MMIO window (QEMU's ECAM host leaves them unassigned); a modern virtio-pci function is vendor 0x1af4 with device id 0x1040 plus the virtio type, and the kernel scans bus 0 reporting each (`virtio entropy at pci slot 1`, `virtio block at pci slot 2`). Done (D2131): the modern virtio-pci transport in `virtio.e` -- `discover` walks the vendor-capability list (cfg_type 1-4) to the common config, notify, ISR and device-config structures; `negotiate` runs the status handshake and accepts only VIRTIO_F_VERSION_1; `read_entropy` builds one split virtqueue (desc/avail/used rings and the buffer in identity-mapped kernel RAM, so VA==PA for DMA), publishes a device-writable descriptor, notifies, and polls the used ring. The kernel's `drive_entropy` prints `entropy N bytes: XX ...`; both suites assert eight random bytes. Verified on both hosts (Linux `neper-self` and Windows `neper-self.exe`), each booting the kernel under QEMU to a different eight-byte sequence. Done (D2132): the virtio-blk driver `block_rw` reuses the transport over a three-descriptor chain (16-byte header the device reads, 512-byte data buffer, one-byte status the device writes), writes a deterministic pattern to sector 0 with VIRTIO_BLK_T_OUT and reads it back with VIRTIO_BLK_T_IN, checking every byte; the queue plumbing is factored into shared `setup_queue`/`ring_wait`, and the block device's BAR is assigned from the cursor the entropy device left so their MMIO windows are disjoint. The kernel prints `block rw ok sector 0: 11 36 5b 80`; both suites assert that exact line. Verified on both hosts under QEMU with a fresh 1 MB disk. Done (D2133): the virtio-console driver `write_console` transmits over port 0's queue 1 without negotiating MULTIPORT (QEMU forwards port-0 tx to the chardev directly); this needed the transport's notify value to carry the queue index (Ring.index), since queue 0 made a literal 0 accidentally correct. The kernel prints `console tx ok` and writes `hello from the neper virtio console` to the port; both suites attach `virtio-serial-pci` with a file-backed `virtconsole`, assert the mark and that the line reached the chardev file, and each driver's BAR is assigned from the previous driver's cursor so the three windows are disjoint. Verified on both hosts under QEMU. Done (D2134): the EL0 memory-access surface -- os.load8/16/32/64, store8/16/32/64 and barrier added to the `neperos` target (resolve.e seed, check.e signatures, runtime_neperos_a64.s bodies, runtime .e regenerated), the floor a user-mode driver needs to touch mapped MMIO and rings without a per-access svc. Gated by g.os==neperos so the compiler's self-compilation is unchanged; surface + lint pass; proven by demo thread Z doing a store/barrier/load round-trip at EL0 (`Z mem ok`), verified by rebuilding neper-self on Windows and booting under QEMU. Done (D2135): the transport's DMA allocation is now a location-agnostic module-level bump pool (pool_set/dma_region) instead of a *mem.Arena, so the same transport runs in the kernel or an EL0 server; read_entropy/block_rw/write_console/setup_queue dropped their arena param and virtio.e no longer imports e.mem; behaviour unchanged, verified under QEMU. Done (D2137): vm.map_range_el0 maps a physical range into an EL0 space at identity VA as Device or Normal memory, splitting the copied kernel L1 block / shared L2 into fresh owned tables (clone_l2/clone_l3) so the untouched remainder stays privileged (confinement); the kernel leaves a driver's addresses in an aux area (put_aux). Proven by prober thread Y reading the entropy device's PCI vendor id (0x1af4) from a kernel-mapped config page at EL0 (`probe vendor ok`), booted under QEMU with no kernel fault. Done (D2138): the entropy driver now runs OUT of the kernel as a capability-confined EL0 user-mode server. The loaded user program moved to neperos/src/init.e so it shares the kernel's modules (`use virtio`); start_entropy_server discovers the device, maps its BAR (Device) + a 128 KB identity DMA pool (Normal) into the server with map_range_el0, leaves common/notify/notify_mult/pool addresses in the aux area, grants a console cap; the `E` branch runs the SAME virtio.read_entropy at EL0 and prints `el0 entropy 8 bytes: ...` (both suites assert it). It holds only its device's frames. Done (D2139): block and console now run as EL0 servers too, so ALL three virtio drivers are capability-confined EL0 user-mode servers and nothing virtio is driven in the kernel. The per-driver kernel setup is one function start_driver_server(..., want_type, name) threading a BAR cursor mmio->E->F->O; drive_entropy/block/console removed; MAX_THREADS raised 16->24. init.e `E`/`F`/`O` share read_device + say_bytes_line (whole line in one os.write so preemption does not interleave output); they print `el0 entropy 8 bytes:`, `el0 block rw ok sector 0: 11 36 5b 80`, `el0 console tx ok`, and the console line reaches the chardev file.
